title: Inside PM at Anthropic: Who Makes It, and Who Doesn’t
author: Nikhyl Singhal
summary: Nikhyl Singhal summarizes his conversation with Dianne Na Penn, who leads product for Anthropic's research and Labs teams, focusing on how she hires, ramps and retains product managers rather than on the models. The piece argues that PM work at a frontier lab is a preview of the job elsewhere: hard first assignments with no scaffolding, an expectation of thoughtful pushback against senior people, and planning in one-month increments. Each lesson is paired with a translation for managers outside the lab, such as pointing new hires to where answers live and making the search part of the job. Na Penn favors people who have a story of pushing through inertia, including first PMs at startups and forward-deployed engineers, over those with a ladder of bigger titles. Early-career PMs are described as effective because they have no process to unlearn. The piece also suggests entering product through customer-facing roles when the PM door is closed.
points: Make the first months deliberately hard: give a real, high-priority assignment early, point to where the answers live, and treat going to find them as the job.
Expect and train new hires to push back, but require homework first, meaning read what was tried and why it died, then challenge with curiosity rather than a hot take.
Hire for evidence of pushing through organizational inertia, such as first-PM-at-a-startup or hard internal turnarounds, over the size of previous titles.
Replace annual OKRs with a short set of assumptions about three to six months out and a one-month plan, while naming the few commitments you are stubborn about.
Early-career people and forward-deployed engineers ramp fast because they carry little process to unlearn, which suggests customer-facing roles as an on-ramp to product.
quotes: Every new hire on Dianne’s team gets the same line in their onboarding plan: the first two months should feel like some of the hardest of your career, and that means you’re doing it right.

The people who settle in fastest are the ones who take that on. The ones who struggle tend to arrive with the reasons they couldn’t do X, Y, and Z, usually because they’re waiting for a structure that isn’t coming.
The habit that trips up PMs from large companies is deference. If your VP says X, you do X, all the way down the chain, and nobody asks whether X is still the right thing.
So the homework comes first: read what was tried and understand why it died. Then push, but in a way that is curious and builds trust.
Managing up used to mean keeping the people above you informed. Now it means having done the reading and being willing to hold an opinion against them.
Each of them is a story about pushing through inertia, with nothing to do with a ladder of bigger titles. That grit, that get-stuff-done attitude, tends to be more powerful than almost anything else.

The OKRs got thrown out quickly, because most assumptions about usage and adoption turned out to be an underestimate. Nobody wanted to spend three months on an annual plan that goes out of date within two weeks.
The version for the rest of us: write down what you’re stubborn about for the next six to twelve months, and treat everything else as a plan that gets rewritten monthly.
